claims.text: The starting nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and are homogeneous solid solutions.
Stability across 473–1923 K is governed by competition between thermally activated atomic diffusion and environment-induced surface segregation.
Atomic diffusion becomes activated at high temperature.
In an oxidative environment, reactive constituents such as Cr or Al preferentially oxidize at the nanoparticle surface.
Cr- or Al-containing alloys can form protective chromia or alumina layers in oxidative environments.
The reactive-element-derived surface oxide is thin, compact, self-limiting, and passivating.
The surface oxide acts as a diffusion barrier that limits further oxidation.
The oxide barrier suppresses bulk atom migration and phase separation in multimetal nanoparticles.
Suppressing atom migration with the oxide layer preserves the nanoparticle's single-phase solid solution and chemical integrity.
Under an inert atmosphere, the absence of an oxide barrier enhances atomic mobility relative to an oxidative atmosphere.
Unpassivated atomic mobility under inert conditions causes elemental segregation and eventual structural decomposition.
Oxidatively heated nanoparticles will show less bulk segregation and better preservation of the solid-solution phase than inertly heated nanoparticles.
Inertly heated nanoparticles will show pronounced rearrangement, phase separation, and detectable lattice-structure changes relative to their initial state.
The prediction requires enough oxide-forming reactive element to generate a protective surface layer.
Nanoparticles lacking protective-oxide-forming elements may not follow the proposed oxidative-versus-inert stability trend.
Extremely small grain or particle sizes can alter diffusion dynamics and thereby change the proposed outcome.
Oxide-formation rates, diffusion rates, and segregation-onset temperatures vary with particle size and elemental composition.
Identical nanoparticle batches should be compared under matched 473–1923 K heating profiles in oxidative and inert atmospheres.
Failure to form an oxide layer, or oxidative and inert samples exhibiting similar segregation and decomposition, would falsify selective oxidation as the governing stability mechanism.
